title: Protect the control plane with CoPP
blurb: Classify traffic aimed at the router itself and rate-limit it so floods can't starve routing and management.
scenario: During a recent ping flood, R1's CPU hit 100 percent, and OSPF neighbors dropped. Use Control Plane Policing to rate-limit traffic sent **to** R1 itself: SSH from the management subnet **10.10.99.0/24** gets **64 kbps**, ICMP gets **8 kbps**, and everything else that reaches the control plane is limited to **32 kbps**.
topology:
Mgmt 10.10.99.0/24 ── R1 (route processor) ── Internet
                     control plane ← CoPP
objectives: Tell apart the management, control and data planes
Classify control plane traffic with ACLs and class maps
Police each class in a policy map
Attach the policy to the control plane and verify it

steps.title: Name the planes
steps.learn: Routers do three kinds of work. The **data plane** forwards transit traffic in hardware. The **control plane** runs routing protocols and other packets addressed to the router. The **management plane** is how admins and tools reach the device. CoPP protects the CPU that handles the control and management planes.
steps.task: Match each kind of traffic to the plane that handles it.

fields.label: A user's web traffic passing through R1
An admin's SSH session to R1

steps.title: Classify the traffic
steps.learn: CoPP uses the Modular QoS CLI. **ACLs** pick packets, **class maps** group them, and a **policy map** acts on each class. In a class map, `match access-group name` points at a named ACL.
steps.task: Create extended ACL **COPP-SSH** permitting TCP from **10.10.99.0/24** to any on port **22**, and ACL **COPP-ICMP** permitting ICMP from any to any. Then create class maps **CM-SSH** and **CM-ICMP** (match-all) that match them.
steps.hint: `ip access-list extended COPP-SSH` with `permit tcp 10.10.99.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 22`; `ip access-list extended COPP-ICMP` with `permit icmp any any`; `class-map match-all CM-SSH` with `match access-group name COPP-SSH`; the same for CM-ICMP.

steps.title: Police each class
steps.learn: `police <bps> conform-action transmit exceed-action drop` passes traffic up to the rate and drops the excess. **class-default** catches everything that no other class matched.
steps.task: Create policy map **PM-COPP**. Police **CM-SSH** to **64000** bps, **CM-ICMP** to **8000** bps and **class-default** to **32000** bps, each transmitting conforming traffic and dropping the excess.
steps.hint: `policy-map PM-COPP`, `class CM-SSH`, `police 64000 conform-action transmit exceed-action drop`, then `class CM-ICMP` with `police 8000 ...` and `class class-default` with `police 32000 ...`.

steps.title: Attach it to the control plane
steps.learn: A CoPP policy is applied **inbound** on the special `control-plane` configuration mode, not on an interface.
steps.task: Apply **PM-COPP** as an input service policy on the control plane.

commands.note: Traffic aimed at R1's CPU is now rate-limited by class.

steps.title: Spot the risk
steps.question: R1 runs OSPF, but no class matches OSPF in this policy. What happens to OSPF hellos during a flood?

options.text: They fall into class-default and compete for its 32 kbps with the flood, so adjacencies could still drop. A real policy gives routing protocols their own generous class.
OSPF is always exempt from CoPP.
options.why: Nothing is exempt. Any traffic punted to the CPU that matches no class lands in class-default.

options.text: They're dropped, because unmatched traffic is denied.
options.why: Unmatched traffic goes to class-default, which this policy polices but doesn't drop outright.

steps.title: Verify the policy
steps.task: Show the policy map applied to the control plane.

commands.output:
Control Plane

  Service-policy input: PM-COPP

    Class-map: CM-ICMP (match-all)
      48211 packets, 3953302 bytes
      5 minute offered rate 312000 bps, drop rate 304000 bps
      Match: access-group name COPP-ICMP
      police:
          cir 8000 bps, bc 1500 bytes
        conformed 1101 packets, 90282 bytes; actions:
          transmit
        exceeded 47110 packets, 3863020 bytes; actions:
          drop
commands.note: The ping flood is being dropped above 8 kbps, so the CPU stays free.

summary: ACLs and class maps for SSH and ICMP, a policy map policing SSH, ICMP and everything else, applied inbound to the control plane, with the drop counters confirming the flood is contained.
